content:
On Monday, Vice President Vance delivered a remarkably earnest analysis of the Netflix romantic comedy starring Lily Collins, hailing it as a 'masterpiece' and even 'the Shakespeare of our era.'

However, Vance also used the show — whose sixth and final season is set to premiere in December — to promote a Republican message of support for marriage and family, while taking aim at the life choices of his fellow millennials.

In a video shared to TikTok, reportedly responding to a friend's criticism of the series, Vance launched into an 'extremely deep' 'meta-analysis' explaining why he considers the show 'genius.'

Vance noted: 'The basic premise is that Lily Collins plays a marketing executive named Emily Cooper, who is a cheerful girl who goes to Paris, has a really cool job, has incredible experiences, drinks great wine, and does all the things you would do in Paris.'

But the show — which sparked debate in its first season over stereotypical portrayals of French people — was, in the words of Trump's running mate, effectively 'a grand cultural critique of millennial decision-making.'

Referring to Lucas Bravo's character Gabriel, Vance said: 'He goes to Paris, and the audience can clearly see he should be with the French chef.'

He continued: 'She should marry this man, and whether in Paris or America, they should start a family and build a life together — that is what they should be doing.'

Watch the video clip here:

Vance said the French chef 'should obviously be with her, rather than her dating all sorts of weird people who keep popping up in her life,' and noted that 'yet both of them made a series of absurd, sometimes funny, and sometimes not entirely convincing wrong decisions, which led to her ending up with a bunch of irrelevant people or just focusing on work, and him ending up with a bunch of irrelevant people or just focusing on work.'

Vance — who has consistently made marriage, parenthood and criticism of childlessness themes of his political career — claimed this point was 'obvious.'

He posited: 'They fall in love, they get married, you two are made for each other, but they keep making outrageous decisions. In a way, that is the best cultural commentary — or rather, cultural critique — of my generation, of millennials.'

Vance concluded the video by recommending: 'You have to watch Emily in Paris,' before declaring: 'It may be an exaggeration, but it really is the Shakespeare of our era.'

Perhaps *Emily in Shakespeare's Homeland*?
